narrative:
The model predicted a 57.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for that year, far below the average of roughly the middle of the class among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 3.70 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model some confidence that you have the academic ability to succeed.

Your LSAT score of 33 was the third most influential piece of information. It sits below the 37.18 average of accepted applicants and therefore nudged the prediction slightly toward failure.

Taken together, the model saw your weak third-year class rank as the dominant signal, only partially offset by your strong college grades. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your class rank in future years, consider a strong bar-preparation plan, and retake the LSAT if possible to bring that score closer to the typical range of admitted students. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection.
